etymology: From Latin cor, the heart, through Old French corage. Courage is heart-strength, and Scripture treats it as something commanded rather than possessed.
biblical_def: Courageous means strong of heart. The remarkable thing in Scripture is that it is always an imperative: God does not congratulate the brave, He commands the fearful. “Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest” (Jos 1:9). The ground is never the man's temperament but the Lord's presence. David charges Solomon the same way for the temple work (1Ch 28:20), and Joab braces the army with it: “be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people” (2Sa 10:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines courageous as brave, bold, daring, intrepid, hardy to encounter difficulties and dangers.
webster_full: COURAGEOUS, a. Brave; bold; daring; intrepid; hardy to encounter difficulties and dangers; adventurous; enterprising.
scriptures: Jos 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.

And David said to Solomon his son, Be strong and of good courage, and do it: fear not, nor be dismayed: for the LORD God, even my God, will be with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee, until thou hast finished all the work for the service of the house of the LORD.
Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God: and the LORD do that which seemeth him good.
Deu 31:6
Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the LORD thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.
corruption_summary: Courage is treated as a personality trait some are issued and others are not, which quietly excuses the fearful from a command God addresses to them directly.
corruption_paragraphs: Every biblical call to courage is spoken to someone currently afraid, and every one supplies a reason outside the man. Joshua is not told to find bravery within; he is told the LORD is with thee whithersoever thou goest. Deuteronomy 31:6 works identically — be strong and of a good courage, fear not… for the LORD thy God, he it is that doth go with thee. Courage in Scripture is a conclusion drawn from a fact about God, which means it is available to timid people.

The counterfeit is bravado, which is courage without the fact. Joab's own sentence guards against it: be of good courage… and the LORD do that which seemeth him good. He resolves to fight hard and leaves the outcome with God, refusing both cowardice and the presumption that resolve guarantees victory.
roots_summary: Hebrew amets (H553), to be strong, alert, courageous; usually paired with chazaq (H2388), to be firm — the doubled imperative of Joshua 1.
roots_lines: Hebrew amets (H553) — be strong, of good courage; Joshua 1:6-9, Deuteronomy 31:6-7.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be firm, strong; the constant companion verb, be strong and of good courage.
Greek tharseo (G2293) — be of good cheer, take courage; Christ's word in the storm, Matthew 14:27.
usage: “Be strong and of a good courage… for the LORD thy God is with thee” — a command with its reason attached.
“Be of good courage, and let us play the men” — resolve that still leaves the outcome with God.
“Fear not… he it is that doth go with thee” — courage addressed to the afraid.

pos: adj. (prudent, sound in judgment; rendering Hebrew bin, Greek sophron)
etymology: From Latin discernere, to separate or distinguish. A discreet man is one who can tell things apart — the opposite of a blunt instrument.
biblical_def: Discreet means sound in practical judgment. Pharaoh asks Joseph for it as a qualification to govern Egypt: “Now therefore let Pharaoh look out a man discreet and wise, and set him over the land” (Gen 41:33). Titus lists it in the curriculum older women teach younger ones (Tit 2:5), and Proverbs supplies its most memorable warning: “As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion” (Pro 11:22). Discretion is what makes every other gift safe to carry.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines discreet as prudent, wise in avoiding errors or evil, and in selecting the best means to accomplish a purpose; circumspect, cautious.
webster_full: DISCREET, a. Prudent; wise in avoiding errors or evil, and in selecting the best means to accomplish a purpose; circumspect; cautious; wary; not rash.
scriptures: Now therefore let Pharaoh look out a man discreet and wise, and set him over the land of Egypt.
Tit 2:5
To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed.
As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion.
And when Jesus saw that he answered discreetly, he said unto him, Thou art not far from the kingdom of God. And no man after that durst ask him any question.
corruption_summary: Discretion reads as timidity in a culture that prizes the unfiltered take, so the discreet are dismissed as evasive and the reckless are praised as authentic.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 11:22 is deliberately grotesque because the point is that a genuine excellence can be ruined by the absence of judgment. The gold is real; the snout is real; the pairing is the tragedy. Gifts, beauty, intelligence, and platform all become liabilities in a person who cannot distinguish the moment, the audience, and the weight of a word.

Pharaoh's instinct is worth noting because it is a pagan king's: he wanted the discreet man in charge of the grain. Administration of other people's food, money, and safety requires the capacity to distinguish, and Scripture makes the same connection when it requires elders to be sober and of good behaviour. Zeal without discretion has wrecked more ministries than opposition ever did.
roots_summary: Hebrew bin (H995), to discern, understand; Greek sophron (G4998), of sound mind, self-controlled — the temperance word behind Titus 2.
roots_lines: Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, consider; Genesis 41:33, a man discreet and wise.
Greek sophron (G4998) — sound-minded, discreet; Titus 2:5, 1 Timothy 3:2 of the bishop.
Hebrew taam (H2940) — taste, discretion; Proverbs 11:22, a fair woman without discretion.
usage: “A man discreet and wise… over the land” — judgment is a governing qualification.
“As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout” — real excellence ruined by no judgment.
“Thou art not far from the kingdom of God” — said to a scribe who answered discreetly.

etymology: From Latin gentilis, of good family — the word once meant well-born, and drifted to mean how the well-born were expected to behave.
biblical_def: Gentle in Scripture is strength that declines to press its advantage. It is required of the overseer — “not a brawler, not covetous” but patient (1Ti 3:3) — and of the Lord's servant generally: “the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient” (2Ti 2:24). Paul describes his own ministry with a nursing image: “we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children” (1Th 2:7). James puts it in the wisdom from above, after purity and peaceableness (Jas 3:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gentle as well-born, mild in manners, soft and refined; placid, not rough, harsh or severe.
webster_full: GENTLE, a. Well-born; of a good family or respectable birth, though not noble.
2. Mild; meek; soft; bland; not rough, harsh or severe.
3. Tame; peaceable; not wild, turbulent or refractory.
scriptures: And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,
But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children:
Jas 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;
corruption_summary: Gentleness is mistaken for weakness or for having no convictions, when Paul commands it precisely of the man whose job is to correct those that oppose themselves.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Timothy 2:24 places gentleness inside a controversy, not outside one. The servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves. The context is doctrinal conflict with real opponents, and gentleness is the prescribed manner of engaging it — because the goal is stated in the next verse: if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth. Harshness may win an argument and lose the man.

Paul's nurse image in 1 Thessalonians 2 shows the cost. A nursing mother's gentleness is not passivity; it is enormous strength subordinated to someone weaker, exercised at her own expense and through the night. Gentle ministry is not low-energy ministry. It is power under discipline, which is why the word sits so close to meekness.
roots_summary: Greek epieikes (G1933), forbearing, yielding, reasonable; epios (G2261), mild — the word of the nursing mother in 1 Thessalonians 2:7.
roots_lines: Greek epieikes (G1933) — gentle, forbearing; 1 Timothy 3:3, Titus 3:2, James 3:17, 1 Peter 2:18.
Greek epios (G2261) — mild, affable; 2 Timothy 2:24 and 1 Thessalonians 2:7.
Greek prautes (G4236) — meekness; the companion virtue, strength under restraint.
usage: “The servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men” — the manner prescribed for controversy.
“Gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children” — strength spent on the weak.
“First pure, then peaceable, gentle” — heavenly wisdom's order.

etymology: Literally without harm. The Greek akeraios means unmixed or unadulterated — the harmlessness of pure metal or unwatered wine, not of feebleness.
biblical_def: Harmless means unmixed, without alloy of malice. Christ pairs it with its opposite temperament so neither can be misused: “be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” (Mat 10:16). Paul repeats the pairing for the church at Philippi: “that ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation” (Php 2:15). Hebrews applies it to Christ Himself as our High Priest: “holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners” (Heb 7:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines harmless as not hurtful or injurious, innoxious; and as unhurt, undamaged, uninjured.
webster_full: HARMLESS, a. Not hurtful or injurious; innoxious; as a harmless medicine.
2. Unhurt; undamaged; uninjured.
3. Innocent; not guilty.
scriptures: Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Php 2:15
That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world;
Heb 7:26
For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens;
For your obedience is come abroad unto all men. I am glad therefore on your behalf: but yet I would have you wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil.
corruption_summary: Harmlessness is read as naivety, so the shrewd despise it and the timid hide behind it — and Christ's deliberate pairing with serpent-wisdom is dropped from both sides.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ gave the two halves together because either alone is a disaster. Serpents without doves produce operators — shrewd, effective, and unsafe. Doves without serpents produce sheep who are eaten in one bite, which is exactly the situation He describes: behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves. The disciple is to be difficult to deceive and impossible to accuse.

Romans 16:19 gives the practical rule for the mind: I would have you wise unto that which is good, and simple concerning evil. Christians often invert it, becoming connoisseurs of evil in the name of engagement and amateurs at good. The harmless man is not ignorant that wolves exist; he simply refuses to become fluent in their methods.
roots_summary: Greek akeraios (G185), unmixed, pure; akakos (G172), without malice — the word for Christ our High Priest in Hebrews 7:26.
roots_lines: Greek akeraios (G185) — unmixed, harmless; Matthew 10:16, Romans 16:19, Philippians 2:15.
Greek akakos (G172) — without evil, guileless; Hebrews 7:26 of Christ, Romans 16:18 of the simple.
Greek phronimos (G5429) — prudent, wise; the serpent half of the pairing.
usage: “Wise as serpents, and harmless as doves” — neither half is safe alone.
“Blameless and harmless… in the midst of a crooked… nation” — purity kept in bad company.
“Holy, harmless, undefiled” — the High Priest who qualifies.

etymology: From Latin liberalis, befitting a free man. In Scripture the word has nothing to do with theology or politics; it means openhanded.
biblical_def: Liberal means generous. Proverbs states the paradox that governs Christian giving: “The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself” (Pro 11:25), a promise placed two verses after the observation that there is that scattereth, and yet increaseth. Isaiah makes liberality a matter of settled purpose rather than impulse: “the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand” (Isa 32:8). Paul uses the word of the Corinthian collection, praising a “liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men” (2Co 9:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines liberal as generous, munificent, bountiful; open-hearted; not selfish, narrow or contracted.
webster_full: LIBERAL, a. Of a free heart; free to give or bestow; not close or contracted; munificent; bountiful; generous; giving largely.
2. Generous; ample; large; as a liberal donation.
3. Not selfish, narrow or contracted; catholic; enlarged.
scriptures: The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.
Isa 32:8
But the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand.
Whiles by the experiment of this ministration they glorify God for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men;
There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty.
corruption_summary: Generosity has been reduced to an impulse the fundraiser must trigger, when Isaiah describes it as a devised policy — the liberal man plans his liberality in advance.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 32:8 supplies the word Christians most need on this subject: deviseth. The liberal deviseth liberal things, and by liberal things shall he stand. Generosity in Scripture is not primarily a response to an appeal but a settled scheme, thought out in advance, which is why Paul had the Corinthians lay by in store on the first day of the week rather than take an emotional collection when he arrived. A giver governed by appeals will be generous exactly as often as someone succeeds in moving him.

Proverbs 11:24-25 states an economics the world calls impossible: there is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty. This is not a technique for getting rich, and reading it that way turns the promise into a transaction. It is a description of how God actually orders the world for the openhanded — the liberal soul shall be made fat — and it stands whether or not the return is visible in this life.
roots_summary: Hebrew nadib (H5081), noble, willing, generous — the same root as the freewill offering; Greek haplotes (G572), singleness, liberality.
roots_lines: Hebrew nadib (H5081) — willing, noble, liberal; Isaiah 32:8, and the willing-hearted of Exodus 35:5.
Hebrew berakah (H1293) — blessing; Proverbs 11:25, the liberal soul shall be made fat.
Greek haplotes (G572) — singleness, liberality; 2 Corinthians 9:11 and 9:13.
usage: “The liberal soul shall be made fat” — an economics the world calls impossible.
“The liberal deviseth liberal things” — generosity as policy, not impulse.
“Your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men” — the collection as evidence of faith.

pos: adj. (humble, of low estate; rendering Hebrew shaphal, Greek tapeinos)
etymology: From low, with the adverbial ending. Scripture makes lowliness a place God visits rather than a status men avoid.
biblical_def: Lowly describes the humble in heart and the low in station, and Scripture treats God's preference between the two as settled: “Though the LORD be high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth afar off” (Psa 138:6). Christ names it as His own temper — the only place He describes His inner life — “learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls” (Mat 11:29). Paul turns it into church policy: “mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate” (Rom 12:16), and Proverbs promises that “with the lowly is wisdom” (Pro 11:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lowly as having a low esteem of one's own worth; humble; meek; free from pride; and as being low in station or rank.
webster_full: LOWLY, a. Having a low esteem of one's own worth; humble; meek; free from pride.
2. Mean; low; wanting dignity or rank.
LOWLY, adv. Humbly; meekly; modestly.
scriptures: Though the LORD be high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth afar off.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits.
Pro 11:2
When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom.
corruption_summary: Lowliness is confused with low self-esteem, so a generation taught to build itself up hears Christ's one self-description as a diagnosis to be cured.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 11:29 deserves more weight than it usually gets, because it is the single verse in which Christ opens His own heart and tells us what is in it. He does not say I am powerful, or I am wise, though both are true. He says I am meek and lowly in heart — and He offers it as the reason His yoke is bearable. The lowliness of Christ is not a lack of self-regard; it is the settled disposition of infinite greatness toward the small.

Romans 12:16 keeps this from remaining an inward feeling. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate; be not wise in your own conceits. The test of lowliness is sociological, not emotional: who is in your house, whose calls you return, whose company you find beneath your time. A church can preach humility for a decade and still sort its people by importance, and Psalm 138 says God sorts the other way round.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaphal (H8217), low, humble; Greek tapeinos (G5011), lowly, of low degree — a word Greeks used contemptuously and the gospel made honourable.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaphal (H8217) — low, humble; Psalm 138:6, Isaiah 57:15, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit.
Greek tapeinos (G5011) — lowly, humble; Matthew 11:29, James 4:6, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
Greek tapeinophrosune (G5012) — lowliness of mind; Philippians 2:3, Ephesians 4:2.
usage: “He hath respect unto the lowly: but the proud he knoweth afar off” — God's settled preference.
“I am meek and lowly in heart” — Christ's only self-description of temper.
“Condescend to men of low estate” — humility tested sociologically.

etymology: From Latin sobrius, not drunk. The New Testament keeps the literal sense but leans on the figurative: a mind not intoxicated by anything.
biblical_def: Sober means clear-headed and self-controlled. Peter attaches it to watchfulness in the presence of a predator: “Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour” (1Pe 5:8), and to prayer itself — “be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer” (1Pe 4:7). Paul makes it eschatological: “let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love” (1Th 5:8). It is required of overseers and of aged men alike (Tit 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sober as temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; not intoxicated; and as having the regular exercise of cool dispassionate reason.
webster_full: SOBER, a. Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; habitually temperate.
2. Not intoxicated or overpowered by spirituous liquors; not drunken.
3. Not mad or insane; having the regular exercise of cool dispassionate reason.
4. Regular; calm; not under the influence of passion; not heated or wild.
scriptures: Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.
But let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation.
Tit 2:2
That the aged men be sober, grave, temperate, sound in faith, in charity, in patience.
corruption_summary: Sobriety is filed as an abstinence issue only, when the New Testament aims it at every intoxicant of the mind — outrage, appetite, spectacle, and the endless feed.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter's pairing tells us what sobriety is for: be sober, be vigilant, because a lion is hunting. A drunk man is not primarily immoral; he is unable to perceive danger accurately or respond to it quickly, and that incapacity is the point of the metaphor. Anything that leaves a Christian slow to notice temptation, dulled to conscience, and reactive rather than watchful has done the work of drink, whatever it is called.

The connection to prayer in 1 Peter 4:7 is the one most often missed. Be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer — a scattered, over-stimulated mind cannot pray, and no amount of sincerity compensates. Much of what Christians diagnose as a prayer problem is a sobriety problem, and the remedy is not more resolve at the moment of prayer but fewer intoxicants during the day.
roots_summary: Greek nepho (G3525), to be sober, unintoxicated, watchful; sophron (G4998), sound-minded — the two strands of the word in the epistles.
roots_lines: Greek nepho (G3525) — to be sober, watchful; 1 Peter 1:13, 4:7, 5:8, 1 Thessalonians 5:6.
Greek sophron (G4998) — of sound mind, discreet; Titus 2:2, 1 Timothy 3:2.
Greek sophroneo (G4993) — to think soberly; Romans 12:3, not to think more highly than he ought.
usage: “Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil…” — sobriety is threat-perception.
“Be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer” — a dulled mind cannot pray.
“Let us, who are of the day, be sober” — clear-headedness as an eschatological posture.

etymology: From Latin temperare, to mix in due proportion. Temperance is not abstinence but proportion — the right amount of the right thing.
biblical_def: Temperate means self-restrained. Paul draws the picture from athletics: “every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible” (1Co 9:25). The point is that unbelievers already discipline themselves for perishable prizes, which leaves the intemperate Christian without excuse. It is required of the elder — “a bishop must be blameless… sober, just, holy, temperate” (Tit 1:8) — and Peter lists it in the ladder of Christian growth (2Pe 1:6). Felix trembled when Paul reasoned of it (Act 24:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines temperate as moderate, not excessive; moderate in the indulgence of the appetites and passions; and cool, calm, not marked by passion.
webster_full: TEMPERATE, a. Moderate; not excessive; as temperate heat.
2. Moderate in the indulgence of the appetites and passions; as temperate in eating and drinking.
3. Cool; calm; not marked with passion; not violent.
scriptures: And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
Tit 1:8
But a lover of hospitality, a lover of good men, sober, just, holy, temperate;
And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness;
And as he reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time; when I have a convenient season, I will call for thee.
corruption_summary: Self-control is treated as repression by a culture built on appetite, while the same culture demands ferocious discipline for fitness and career — proving the objection is selective.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's argument in 1 Corinthians 9 is unanswerable precisely because it appeals to what everyone already accepts. The athlete denies himself food, sleep, and comfort for a wreath that will be brown within the month. Nobody calls him repressed; they call him committed. The Christian who will not govern his appetites for an incorruptible crown is therefore not liberated but inconsistent, applying a discipline he already believes in everywhere except where it matters most.

Acts 24:25 shows the word's edge. Paul reasoned of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come, and Felix trembled — a Roman governor living with another man's wife heard self-control preached and felt the floor move. Temperance is not a mild virtue for mild people; preached honestly to the powerful, it is the thing that makes them ask for another appointment at a more convenient season.
roots_summary: Greek egkrates (G1468), self-controlled, literally holding oneself in; the noun egkrateia (G1466) is the temperance of Galatians 5:23, a fruit of the Spirit.
roots_lines: Greek egkrates (G1468) — self-controlled; Titus 1:8 of the bishop.
Greek egkrateia (G1466) — temperance, self-control; Galatians 5:23, 2 Peter 1:6, Acts 24:25.
Greek egkrateuomai (G1467) — to exercise self-control; 1 Corinthians 9:25 of the athlete.
usage: “Every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things” — the athlete indicts the intemperate believer.
“Sober, just, holy, temperate” — a standing requirement for office.
“He reasoned of… temperance… Felix trembled” — self-control preached to power.

pos: adj. (of moral strength and worth; rendering Hebrew chayil)
etymology: From Latin virtus, manliness, strength, excellence. The Hebrew word behind it, chayil, is a military term for force and ability.
biblical_def: Virtuous in Scripture means strong in moral worth, and the Hebrew is bracing: chayil is the word for an army, for valour, for substance. “Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies” (Pro 31:10) is therefore not a portrait of decorative gentility but of formidable capability under God. Boaz uses it of Ruth — “all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman” (Rut 3:11) — and Proverbs makes the domestic consequence plain: “A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband” (Pro 12:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines virtuous as morally good, acting in conformity to the moral law; and as being efficacious by inherent qualities.
webster_full: VIRTUOUS, a. Morally good; acting in conformity to the moral law; practising the moral duties, and abstaining from vice.
2. Being in conformity to the moral or divine law; as a virtuous action.
3. Chaste; applied to women.
4. Efficacious by inherent qualities; as virtuous herbs.
scriptures: Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.
Rut 3:11
And now, my daughter, fear not; I will do to thee all that thou requirest: for all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman.
Pro 12:4
A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones.
Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 31 is read either as an impossible standard that shames women or as a decorative ideal that patronizes them — both miss that chayil is the vocabulary of strength.
corruption_paragraphs: The word choice governs the whole chapter. Chayil describes armies, wealth, and valour; when it is applied to a woman the picture that follows matches — she buys a field, plants a vineyard, trades profitably, arms herself with strength, opens her hand to the poor, and laughs at the time to come. This is not a wife decorating a household but a woman deploying formidable competence within it. Reading the chapter as a checklist of chores misses the genre; it is a poem in praise of strength.

Ruth is the flesh on the definition, and the detail matters: she was a Moabitess, a widow, and destitute, gleaning behind reapers for survival. What made the whole city call her a woman of chayil was not her circumstances but her covenant loyalty to Naomi and her willingness to work. Virtue in Scripture is available to the poor, which is precisely what a decorative reading of Proverbs 31 makes impossible.
roots_summary: Hebrew chayil (H2428), strength, force, ability, an army; used of Ruth, of the Proverbs 31 woman, and of mighty men of valour.
roots_lines: Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, valour, substance; Proverbs 31:10, Ruth 3:11, and the men of valour throughout Judges and Samuel.
Greek arete (G703) — virtue, moral excellence; 2 Peter 1:5, add to your faith virtue.
Hebrew ishshah chayil — woman of strength; the phrase Boaz applies to Ruth.
usage: “Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies” — strength, not decoration.
“Thou art a virtuous woman” — said of a destitute foreign widow.
“A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband” — the household consequence.

etymology: From Greek zelos, heat, fervour. Zeal is a temperature, and Scripture is careful to ask what the heat is for.
biblical_def: Zealous means burning with earnestness. Scripture treats it as a raw force needing direction: Paul testifies that his countrymen “have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2), and he had himself persecuted the church out of exactly that zeal. Rightly aimed, it is required — Christ redeems for Himself “a peculiar people, zealous of good works” (Tit 2:14) — and its absence draws the harshest verdict in the letters to the churches: “because thou art lukewarm… be zealous therefore, and repent” (Rev 3:16,19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines zealous as warmly engaged or ardent in the pursuit of an object; and warmly engaged in religion.
webster_full: ZEALOUS, a. Warmly engaged or ardent in the pursuit of an object.
2. Warm; ardent; fervent; as zealous love; zealous devotion.
scriptures: Rom 10:2
For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
Tit 2:14
Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.
Rev 3:19
As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.
Gal 4:18
But it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing, and not only when I am present with you.
corruption_summary: Two failures sit side by side: zeal without knowledge, which does damage in God's name, and knowledge without zeal, which Christ threatens to spew out of His mouth.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 10:2 is Paul's charitable and devastating assessment of his own nation: they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge. He is not calling them insincere; he is saying sincerity is not the question. Zeal is a fire, and a fire in the hearth warms the house while the same fire in the roof destroys it. Every persecution the church has suffered from religious people, and every harm the church has done to others, has run on genuine zeal aimed wrongly.

But the opposite error is the one Christ addresses to a church rather than to unbelievers, and He uses stronger language for it. Laodicea was neither cold nor hot, and the remedy prescribed is not more information but temperature: be zealous therefore, and repent. A congregation that has traded fervour for respectability has not become mature; it has become the one thing in Revelation that provokes nausea.
roots_summary: Greek zelotes (G2207), a zealot, one burning with zeal; zeloo (G2206), to be fervent — capable of holy jealousy or of envy, depending on its object.
roots_lines: Greek zelotes (G2207) — zealous one; Acts 22:3, Titus 2:14, 1 Corinthians 14:12.
Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal, fervour; John 2:17, the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up.
Greek zeloo (G2206) — to be zealous; Revelation 3:19, and Galatians 4:18, it is good to be zealously affected always in a good thing.
usage: “A zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” — sincerity is not the question.
“A peculiar people, zealous of good works” — zeal with an assigned direction.
“Be zealous therefore, and repent” — the cure for lukewarm.

etymology: From stead, a place, and fast, fixed — fixed in its place. The KJV spelling preserves the older form of steadfast.
biblical_def: Stedfast means firmly fixed and immovable. Hebrews makes hope the anchor: “which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast” (Heb 6:19), the metaphor requiring that the anchor be fixed in something outside the ship. Paul's charge to the Corinthians is built on the resurrection he has just proved: “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” (1Co 15:58). Peter warns that the unstable wrest the scriptures to their own destruction and urges believers to resist the devil “stedfast in the faith” (1Pe 5:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines steadfast as fast fixed, firm, firmly fixed or established; constant, firm, resolute, not fickle or wavering.
webster_full: STEADFAST, a. Fast fixed; firm; firmly fixed or established; as the steadfast globe of earth.
2. Constant; firm; resolute; not fickle or wavering.
3. Steady; constant; not variable.
scriptures: Heb 6:19
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;
Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Whom resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world.
Col 1:23

If ye continue in the faith grounded and settled, and be not moved away from the hope of the gospel, which ye have heard, and which was preached to every creature which is under heaven; whereof I Paul am made a minister;
corruption_summary: Constancy is read as rigidity in a culture that prizes reinvention, so a church prone to reinvent its convictions every decade calls its instability growth.
corruption_paragraphs: The anchor image in Hebrews 6 is precise about where stability comes from. An anchor is useless if it is fastened to the ship; it must grip something the storm cannot move. The passage says this hope entereth into that within the veil, whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus — the anchor is fixed inside the sanctuary of heaven. Steadfastness is therefore not a strength of grip in the believer but a strength of hold in the object.

1 Corinthians 15:58 shows why the doctrine of resurrection is not abstract. Paul spends a chapter proving that the dead rise, then draws one practical conclusion: therefore, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord. Constancy in unrewarding work is only rational if there is a resurrection. Take that away and drifting is the sensible response.
roots_summary: Greek bebaios (G949), firm, reliable, guaranteed; hedraios (G1476), seated, settled — from hedra, a seat.
roots_lines: Greek bebaios (G949) — firm, sure; Hebrews 6:19, 2 Peter 1:19, a more sure word of prophecy.
Greek hedraios (G1476) — settled, steadfast; 1 Corinthians 15:58, Colossians 1:23.
Greek stereos (G4731) — solid, firm; 2 Timothy 2:19, the foundation of God standeth sure.
usage: “An anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast” — fixed in something outside the ship.
“Be ye stedfast, unmoveable… your labour is not in vain” — resurrection makes constancy rational.
“Whom resist stedfast in the faith” — the posture against the adversary.

pos: adv. (with careful attention; rendering Hebrew shanan, Greek epimelos)
etymology: From Latin diligere, to love or choose — diligence is care that arises from valuing a thing, not from mere duty.
biblical_def: Diligently describes attention proportioned to worth. The Shema commands it of household teaching: “thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house” (Deu 6:7) — the Hebrew verb means to sharpen, to whet, repeating until the truth has an edge. Hebrews makes it the condition of pleasing God: “he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him” (Heb 11:6). Proverbs makes it economic: “the hand of the diligent maketh rich” (Pro 10:4), and the woman who lost a coin lit a candle and sought diligently till she found it (Luk 15:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines diligently as with steady application and care; with industry or assiduity; not carelessly, not negligently.
webster_full: DILIGENTLY, adv. With steady application and care; with industry or assiduity; not carelessly; not negligently.
scriptures: Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Heb 11:6
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
Pro 10:4
He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich.
Luk 15:8
Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?
corruption_summary: Diligence is admired in careers and abandoned in discipleship, so the same person who trains for a marathon expects to know God by accident.
corruption_paragraphs: The Hebrew verb in Deuteronomy 6:7 is shanan, to sharpen or whet, as one puts an edge on a blade by repeated strokes. Household instruction is therefore not a lecture delivered once but the same truth applied again and again until it cuts. The verse then locates the strokes in ordinary life — when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. Parents who outsource this to an hour on Sunday have not delegated the task; they have abandoned the method.

Hebrews 11:6 keeps diligence from becoming works-righteousness by naming what is actually rewarded: God is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him. The diligence is in the seeking of a Person, not the accumulation of religious performance, and the promise is that such seeking is never wasted. The candle-and-broom of Luke 15 is the picture — the woman does not wait for the coin to turn up; she lights, sweeps, and seeks diligently till she find it.
roots_summary: Hebrew shanan (H8150), to whet or sharpen; Greek epimelos (G1960), carefully; ekzeteo (G1567), to seek out earnestly.
roots_lines: Hebrew shanan (H8150) — to sharpen, to teach incisively; Deuteronomy 6:7.
Greek ekzeteo (G1567) — to seek out; Hebrews 11:6, them that diligently seek him.
Greek epimelos (G1960) — carefully, diligently; Luke 15:8, and she seek diligently till she find it.
usage: “Thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” — repetition that puts an edge on truth.
“A rewarder of them that diligently seek him” — the object is a Person.
“Seek diligently till she find it” — the candle and the broom.
